STUDIA MATHEMATICA
        Online First version




        Invariant means on Abelian groups capture
  complementability of Banach spaces in their second duals
                                              by

                         Adam P. Goucher (Cambridge) and
                         Tomasz Kania (Praha and Kraków)

     Abstract. Let X be a Banach space. Then X is complemented in the bidual X ∗∗ if
and only if there exists an invariant mean `∞ (G, X) → X with respect to a free Abelian
group G of rank equal to the cardinality of X ∗∗ , and this happens if and only if there exists
an invariant mean with respect to the additive group of X ∗∗ . This improves upon previous
results due to Bustos Domecq (2002) and the second-named author (2017), where certain
idempotent semigroups of cardinality equal to the cardinality of X ∗∗ were considered, and
answers a question of J. M. F. Castillo (private communication) that was also considered
by Kania (2017). En route to the proof of the main result, we endow the family of all
finite-dimensional subspaces of an infinite-dimensional vector space with a structure of
a free commutative monoid with the property that the product of two subspaces contains
the respective subspaces, which is possibly of interest in itself.

   1. Introduction and the main result. Every Banach space X embeds
canonically (linearly and isometrically) into its second dual space X ∗∗ via
the map κX : X → X ∗∗ defined by
                          hκX x, f i = hf, xi (x ∈ X, f ∈ X ∗ ),
so that it is customary to identify X with a closed subspace of X ∗∗ . The
question of when is X complemented in X ∗∗ (that is, when does there exist
a bounded linear projection from X ∗∗ onto the image of κX ) is a frequently
recurring problem in Banach space theory, as Banach spaces complemented
in their biduals enjoy various, otherwise often unavailable, averaging prop-
erties such as the existence of vector valued invariant means with respect
to amenable semigroups. Banach spaces complemented in their biduals in-
clude, besides reflexive spaces, dual spaces and weakly sequentially complete
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: Primary 43A07; Secondary 46B50.
Key words and phrases: amenable semigroup, invariant mean, vector-valued mean, prin-
ciple of local reflexivity, Banach space complemented in bidual, free Abelian group, free
commutative monoid.

Banach lattices; c0 , the space of sequences converging to 0, is the most promi-
nent example of a space not complemented in its bidual.
    Let X be a Banach space, (S, ·) a semigroup, and λ ≥ 1. A bounded
linear operator M : `∞ (S, X) → X of norm at most λ such that for every
x ∈ X, s ∈ S, and for all f ∈ `∞ (S, X) one has
 (i) M (x1S ) = x;
(ii) M (f ) = M (s f ) = M (fs ),
is called an X-valued invariant λ-mean on S. Here, `∞ (S, X) denotes the
Banach space of all bounded X-valued functions on S, x1S stands for the
function constantly equal to x on S, and s f (t) = f (s · t) and fs (t) = (t · s)
(s, t ∈ S). When there is no need to emphasise the constant λ, M is simply
called an X-valued invariant mean on S.
     A semigroup is amenable if it admits an X-valued 1-mean with X one-
dimensional (namely, the scalar field). By the Markov–Kakutani fixed-point
theorem, all commutative semigroups are amenable. In the literature, means
invariant with respect to the additive monoid of natural numbers (with zero)
are called Banach limits (vector-valued Banach limits when dim X ≥ 2).
     Invariant means with respect to more complicated semigroups were em-
ployed by Pełczyński, who proved that for a Banach space X, if Y ⊆ X
is a closed subspace which is complemented in Y ∗∗ and there exists a Lip-
schitz map r : X → Y such that r(y) = y for y ∈ Y , then Y is (linearly)
complemented in X ([Pe68, pp. 61–62], see also [Ben04, Theorem 3.3]).
     Suppose that S is an amenable semigroup and X is a Banach space
that is complemented in X ∗∗ . Then one can construct an X-valued invariant
λ-mean on S as follows. Let m be a (scalar-valued) invariant mean on S. We
define a map M f : `∞ (S, X) → X ∗∗ by

             hM
              ff, ϕi = m, hϕ, f (·)i      (ϕ ∈ X ∗ , f ∈ `∞ (S, X)).
Since kmk = 1, M
               f is a norm-one bounded linear operator. If P is a projection
       ∗∗
from X onto the canonical copy of X, then
                             M = κ−1 P Mf
                                         X
is an X-valued invariant kP k-mean on S.
    In order to prove that the converse holds true as well, in [Bus02, Ka17]
the existence of an invariant mean on a certain idempotent semigroup S was
assumed; the semigroup S comprises pairs (F, ε), where F ⊂ X ∗∗ is a finite-
dimensional subspace and ε > 0; the semigroup operation was defined as
(F, ε) · (G, δ) = (F + G, min{ε, δ}); related questions were also considered in
[Lu17].
    In this note we consider the following question communicated privately
to the second-named author by J. M. F. Castillo:
                  Complementability of Banach spaces in the bidual              3

      Suppose that a Banach space X admits an invariant mean with
      respect to every/some Abelian group. Must X be complemented
      in X ∗∗ ?
    The question arises from the observation that the semigroup S used to
prove the existence of a projection from X ∗∗ onto X is idempotent, so in
a sense, it is as far from being a (subset of a) group as possible. In the present
paper we demonstrate that free Abelian groups of large enough rank suffice
to prove the existence of a projection from the bidual.
   Theorem A. Let X be a Banach space and λ ≥ 1. Then the following
assertions are equivalent:
  (i) X is complemented in X ∗∗ by a projection of norm at most λ;
 (ii) for every amenable semigroup S there exists an X-valued invariant λ-
      mean on S;
(iii) when G is a free Abelian group of rank |X ∗∗ |, there exists an X-valued
      invariant λ-mean on G;
(iv) there exists an X-valued invariant λ-mean on the additive group of X ∗∗ .
    The implication (i)⇒(ii) has already been briefly explained and may be
found, for example, in [Bus02, Theorem 1]. The implications (ii)⇒(iii) and
(ii)⇒(iv) are clear. We shall prove the implications (iii)⇒(i) and (iv)⇒(iii)
in the subsequent section.
    Every Abelian group is a quotient of a free Abelian group, so by Lem-
ma 2.3(ii), clause (iii) in Theorem A is not weaker than the assertion that for
every Abelian group G of cardinality X ∗∗ there exists an X-valued invariant
λ-mean on G.
    The additive group of X ∗∗ may seem large, since already for separable
Banach spaces that contain an isomorphic copy of `1 , it has the cardinality
of the power set of the continuum; however, this is unavoidable. Indeed, it
follows from [Ka17, Corollary 1.4] that the Banach space X = `c∞ (Γ ) of
all countably supported bounded functions on an uncountable set Γ (en-
dowed with the supremum norm) admits invariant means with respect to all
countable amenable semigroups, yet X is not complemented in X ∗∗ [PS62].
    Remark 1.1. We remark in passing that the mere existence of an X-
valued invariant mean with respect to some commutative semigroup (that
could be chosen as large as one wishes) is not sufficient for X to be comple-
mented in X ∗∗ . To see this, fix an arbitrary Banach space X (not necessarily
complemented in X ∗∗ ) and let (S, ·) be a semigroup with an element 0 ∈ S
such that 0 · s = s · 0 = 0 for all s ∈ S. Define M : `∞ (S, X) → X by
M f = f (0). Certainly, M is a norm-one linear operator and M (x1S ) = x
for any x ∈ X. Moreover, M fs = fs (0) = f (0 · s) = f (0) = M f = M s f for
any s ∈ S.
4                          A. P. Goucher and T. Kania

    It is known that if a separable Banach space X has a monotone ba-
sis (or more generally, the Metric Approximation Property), then X is 1-
complemented in X ∗∗ if and only if there exists an X-valued 1-mean on N
(an X-valued Banach limit); see [GP18, Corollary 4.2.6]. It follows from
Lemma 2.2 that this is equivalent to the existence of an X-valued invariant
1-mean on Z. Thus, at least for very well-behaved separable Banach spaces
complementability in the bidual can be indeed witnessed by the group of
integers (the free abelian group of rank one).
    The key result needed to establish Theorem A is related to the possi-
bility of turning the family of all finite-dimensional subspaces of X ∗∗ into
a cancellative monoid.
    Theorem B. Let V be an infinite-dimensional vector space over an arbi-
trary field. Denote by Fin V the set of all finite-dimensional subspaces of V .
Then there exists a binary operation ∗ on Fin V such that
 (i) (Fin V, ∗) is a free commutative monoid;
(ii) for any F, G ∈ Fin V we have F, G ⊆ F ∗ G.
Consequently, the Grothendieck group of (Fin V, ∗) is a free Abelian group.
    It is quite clear that there is no counterpart of Theorem B for a finite-
dimensional vector space V , as seen by taking three different hyperplanes
W1 , W2 , W3 in V and noticing that V = W1 ∗ W3 = W2 ∗ W3 , which makes
cancellativity impossible to satisfy.
    It is noteworthy that the proof of Theorem B makes use of Zermelo’s
well-ordering principle and does depend on the chosen well-ordering of the
set Fin X ∗∗ \{0}, but the resulting group is always free Abelian of rank |X ∗∗ |.

    2. Auxiliary facts. We denote by N = {0, 1, 2, . . .} the additive monoid
of non-negative integers. As such, it is a submonoid of the group of integers Z.
A multiset is formally a pair (Γ, ϕ), where Γ is an arbitrary non-empty set
and ϕ : Γ → {1, 2, . . .} counts the multiplicity of a given item in the multiset.
    An Abelian group G is free if it is free as a module over Z; then G is
isomorphic to the direct sum Z(α) of α-many copies of the group Z for some
cardinal α, called the rank of G. In particular, two uncountable free Abelian
groups of the same cardinality are isomorphic. Besides free Abelian groups,
we will require the notion of a free commutative monoid, that is, a monoid
isomorphic to the direct sum N(α) of α-many copies of N for some cardinal α.
    Let (S, +) be a commutative semigroup. Then S embeds into a group if
and only if S is cancellative. In the latter case, S embeds into its Grothendieck
group G(S), comprising the equivalence classes of the relation ∼ on S × S
given by
        (s1 , t1 ) ∼ (s2 , t2 ) ⇐⇒ s1 + t2 = t1 + s2 (s1 , s2 , t1 , t2 ∈ S).
                  Complementability of Banach spaces in the bidual                 5

Thus, formally G(S) = {s−t : s, t ∈ S} and 0S = 0G(S) belongs to S ∩(−S) if
S is already a monoid. Of course, Z is the Grothendieck group of N and more
generally Z(α) is the Grothendieck group of the free commutative monoid
N(α) for any cardinal number α.
    All commutative semigroups are amenable, yet subsemigroups of ame-
nable groups need not be amenable. In the vector-valued case, we need to
justify separately the possibility of passing to a subsemigroup, even in the
commutative case.
    We shall require the following lemma concerning invariant means on
groups that admit the infinite cyclic group as a quotient.
    Lemma 2.1. Let X be a Banach space and let G be a group with a sur-
jective homomorphism θ : G → Z. Suppose that M : `∞ (G, X) → X is an X-
valued invariant mean. Then M f = 0 for any function f supported on the
kernel of θ.
    Proof. Assume otherwise. Let g ∈ G satisfy θ(g) = 1. Then for each
n ∈ N and t ∈ G with θ(t) 6= −n, we have θ(tg n ) 6= 0, and therefore
fgn (t) = f (tg n ) = 0. Hence, the functions {fgn : n ∈ N} have pairwise
disjoint supports.
    By the translation-invariance, M (fgn ) = M (f ) for every n ∈ N, so
                   M (fg + fg2 + fg3 + · · · + fgn ) = nM (f ).
As the summands have pairwise disjoint supports, the sum has the same
supremum norm as f itself (and in particular is constant as a function of n).
On the other hand, the norm of nM (f ) grows without bound as n → ∞,
contradicting the continuity of M .
    Lemma 2.2. Let X be a Banach space and let λ ≥ 1. If for some α there
exists an X-valued invariant λ-mean on Z(α) , then there exists such a mean
on N(α) too.
    Proof. Let M : `∞ (Z(α) , X) → X be an X-valued invariant λ-mean. For
t ∈ Z(α) we define |t| coordinatewise, that is, |t|(i) = |t(i)| for i ∈ α. Let
M 0 : `∞ (N(α) , X) → X be given by M 0 (f ) = M (f 0 ), where f 0 (t) := f (|t|) for
t ∈ Z(α) and f ∈ `∞ (Z(α) , X). In particular, for f = x1N(α) (x ∈ X), we have
                     M 0 f = M 0 (x1N(α) ) = M (x1Z(α) ) = x.
    Moreover, f 0 and f have the same supremum norm by definition; conse-
quently, the operator norm of M 0 is upper-bounded by the operator norm
of M , which in turn is no greater than λ. To show that M 0 is an X-valued
invariant λ-mean, it remains to show that M 0 is translation-invariant. Since
every g ∈ N(α) can be written as a finite sum of ‘basis elements’ ei where
i ∈ α, it suffices to show that for every i ∈ α and every f ∈ `∞ (N(α) , X), we
have M 0 (fei ) = M 0 (f ).
6                            A. P. Goucher and T. Kania

     Let πi : Z(α) → Z be the ‘projection map’ homomorphism which satisfies
πi (ei ) = 1 and πi (ej ) = 0 for all j 6= i. For a predicate φ : Z → {true, false}
and h ∈ `∞ (Z(α) , X), we define h[φ(πi )] to be the restriction of h to the
values where the predicate is true:
                                         (
                                           h(x) if φ(πi (x)),
                        h[φ(πi )](x) :=
                                           0      otherwise.
Then we can write
            f 0 = f 0 [πi ≤ −2] + f 0 [πi = −1] + f 0 [πi = 0] + f 0 [πi ≥ 1]
and similarly
                     (fei )0 = (fei )0 [πi ≤ −1] + (fei )0 [πi ≥ 0].
Observe the following:
• f 0 [πi ≤ −2] is a translate of (fei )0 [πi ≤ −1], so
                       M (f 0 [πi ≤ −2]) = M ((fei )0 [πi ≤ −1]);
• f 0 [πi ≥ 1] is a translate of (fei )0 [πi ≥ 0], so
                         M (f 0 [πi ≥ 1]) = M ((fei )0 [πi ≥ 0]);
• M (f 0 [πi = 0]) is zero by Lemma 2.1;
• M (f 0 [πi = 1]) is also zero, by Lemma 2.1 combined with translation-
  invariance of M .
By linearity of M , it follows that M (f 0 ) = M ((fei )0 ), and therefore (by
definition) M 0 (f ) = M 0 (fei ). The result follows.
    It is a standard fact that subgroups and quotients of amenable discrete
groups are amenable. Using exactly the same ideas one can prove that if
a Banach space admits an invariant mean with respect to a group, then it
also does so with respect to subgroups and quotients of the group.
   Lemma 2.3. Let X be a Banach space and let G be a group with a nor-
mal subgroup H. Suppose that there exists an X-valued invariant λ-mean
M : `∞ (G, X) → X on G. Then
  (i) there exists an X-valued invariant λ-mean on H;
 (ii) there exists an X-valued invariant λ-mean on G/H;
(iii) if moreover S and T are isomorphic semigroups and there exists an
      X-valued invariant mean on S, then there exists such a mean on T too.
                                                                 F

    Clause (iii) is quite trivial. Suppose that θ : T → S is an isomorphism
and M : `∞ (S, X) → X a mean on S. Then N f = M (f ◦ θ) (f ∈ `∞ (T, X))
is an invariant mean on T .
   We shall require the principle of local reflexivity due to Lindenstrauss
and Rosenthal [LR69], which we state for future reference.
    Theorem 2.4. Let X be a Banach space and let F ⊂ X ∗∗ be a finite-
dimensional subspace. Then for each ε ∈ (0, 1) there exists a linear map
PFε : F → κX (X) such that
 (i) (1 − ε)kxk ≤ kPFε xk ≤ (1 + ε)kxk (x ∈ F );
(ii) PFε x = x for x ∈ F ∩ κX (X).

    3. Proofs of the main results. We start with the proof of Theo-
rem B on which Theorem A relies. The proof proceeds by partitioning
S := Fin V \ {0} (the set of all non-zero finite-dimensional subspaces of
an infinite-dimensional vector space V ) into disjoint sets P and Q. Then, we
construct a bijection between Fin V and the free commutative monoid FP ,
obtaining the operation ∗ by pulling back the monoid operation through this
bijection.
     Proof of Theorem B. We begin by using Zermelo’s well-ordering principle
to construct a bijection θ : S → α, where α is a cardinal number (that is,
an initial ordinal). This induces a well-ordering φ on the collection FS of
finite multisets of elements from S. Specifically, if A ∈ FS contains elements
U1 , . . . , Uk with respective multiplicities c1 , . . . , ck , then we define
                      φ(A) := ω θ(U1 ) · c1 + · · · + ω θ(Uk ) · ck ,
where without loss of generality we have taken θ(U1 ) > · · · > θ(Uk ). The
well-ordering φ on FS is known as colexicographical order, and the order type
is again α.
    FS is a graded monoid, where the grading v(A) = c1 + · · · + ck is the
total number of elements (counted with multiplicity) in the multiset. It is
convenient to define, for each n ∈ N,
                             (n)
                          FS       := {A ∈ FS : v(A) ≥ n}.
                (0)            (1)
In particular, FS = FS , FS is the collection of non-empty multisets in FS ,
      (2)
and FS is the collection of non-empty non-singleton multisets in FS .
                                                                        (2)
   For each β ≤ α, we define an injective partial function gβ : FS → S:
• When β = 0 is the zero ordinal, gβ is the empty partial function.
8                         A. P. Goucher and T. Kania

• When β = γ + is a successor ordinal, gβ is obtained from gγ by extending
  it with another element gβ (A) = W . Here A is defined to be the first (in
                                               (2)
  the colexicographical order φ) element A ∈ FS such that A is not in the
  domain of gγ and no element of A is in the image of gγ . Further W is an
  arbitrary element of S such that
    (1) for all B ( A with v(B) ≥ 2, gγ (B) is a subspace of W (note that
                                           (2)
        the colexicographical ordering on FS ensures that we have already
        defined gγ on all such subsets B);
    (2) each U ∈ A is a subspace of W ;
    (3) W occurs later in the well-ordering on S induced by θ−1 than any
        element in A, any element in any B ∈ dom(gγ ), and any element in
        the image of gγ .
  We have to show that these conditions are consistent. Conditions (1)
  and (2) merely specify that W contains a particular finite-dimensional
  subspace W 0 (the Minkowski sum of all U ∈ A and all gγ (B) where
  B ( A with v(B) ≥ 2); since V is infinite-dimensional, the collection
  {W ∈ Fin V : W 0 ⊆ W } has the same cardinality as Fin V itself. Ow-
  ing to our choice of an initial ordinal for the well-ordering, condition (3)
  only eliminates a strictly smaller set of candidates for W , so the set of
  admissible W is non-empty.
• When β is a limit ordinal, gβ is the union of the partial functions gγ (for
  all γ < β).
    Let Q be the image of gα and let P := S \ Q. We claim that the domain
                  (2)

            (2)

in the transfinite recursion and therefore belongs to the domain of gα .
                                                                      (2)
    In the other direction, suppose that A ∈ dom(gα ) and A ∈   / FP . Then
there exists an element W ∈ A such that W ∈ Q. Now, A was introduced
into the domain of gα at some successor ordinal β = γ + of the transfinite
recursion. By the definition of A, W cannot be in the image of gγ , so W must
have appeared at some later step of the recursion. However, that contradicts
condition (3), which forces W to be later in the well-ordering than (and
therefore not equal to) any element of A.
                     (2)                                               (2)
    Consequently, FP = dom(gα ) so we have a total function gα : FP → Q.
    We extend gα to a bijection f : FP → Fin V by setting
• f (∅) := {0};
• f ({V }) := V for all singleton sets {V } where V ∈ P;
• f (A) := gα (A) if v(A) ≥ 2.

At this point, we define a binary operation ∗ : Fin V × Fin V → Fin V by
                     U1 ∗ U2 := f (f −1 (U1 ) t f −1 (U2 )),
where t is the ‘disjoint union’ operation that makes FP into a free commu-
tative monoid. This immediately establishes part (i) of the proposition, that
(Fin V, ∗) is a free commutative monoid.
    It remains to show part (ii) of Theorem B, that for any F, G ∈ Fin V
we have F, G ⊆ F ∗ G. We can assume that neither F nor G is the trivial
space {0}, as this is the identity of the operation ∗ and the statement would
trivially hold.
    Consequently, v(f −1 (F )) ≥ 1 and v(f −1 (G)) ≥ 1, so v(f −1 (F ∗ G)) ≥ 2.
                                           (2)
This means that A := f −1 (F ∗G) is in FP and therefore appeared (together
with the space W := F ∗ G) in the recursion. We shall show that F is
a subspace of W := F ∗ G:

• If v(f −1 (F )) = 1, then f −1 (F ) is the singleton set {F }. Hence F ∈ A,
  and therefore F is a subspace of W by condition (2) in the recursion.
• If v(f −1 (F )) ≥ 2, then f −1 (F ) = B ( A and F = f (B) is a subspace of
  W by condition (1) in the recursion.

   By symmetry, it follows that G is also a subspace of F ∗ G, establishing
the truth of Theorem B.

   We are now ready to prove Theorem A.

    Proof of Theorem A. We are now to prove the implications (iii)⇒(i) and
(iv)⇒(iii).
    Without loss of generality we may assume that X is infinite-dimensional.
To prove the former implication, consider the free commutative monoid

    In order to prove (iv)⇒(iii), we observe that X ∗∗ is in particular a Q-vec-

Lemma 2.3 there is an X-valued invariant mean on a free Abelian group of
rank |X ∗∗ |.
    3.1. Countable amenable groups. As already explained, separable
Banach spaces with the Metric Approximation Property are 1-complemented
in their biduals if and only if they admit an invariant 1-mean on the group
of integers. If one replaces the Metric Approximation Property with the
γ-Bounded Approximation Property (with parameter γ ≥ 1), then comple-
mentation in the bidual is still characterised by the existence of an invariant
mean on the group of integers but the correspondence between the norm of
the mean and the upper bound for the norm of a projection from the bidual
is impeded by the parameter γ. Nonetheless, we do not know the answer to
the following question.
                    Complementability of Banach spaces in the bidual                    11

      Let X be a separable Banach space. Suppose that for some count-
      ably infinite amenable group G there exists an X-valued invariant
      mean on G. Is X complemented in the bidual X ∗∗ ?
   Acknowledgements. The second-named author wishes to express
thanks to Radosław Łukasik for numerous conversations concerning the prob-
lem. Morever, we thank the referee for his or her extremely thorough report.
